question: A 21-year-old female is brought to the emergency department by her roommate. Her roommate says that the patient has been acting “strangely” for the past 10 days. She has noticed that the patient has been moving and talking on the phone at all hours of the night. She doesn’t think that the patient sleeps more than one to two hours a night. She also spends hours pacing up and down the apartment, talking about “trying to save the world.” She also notices that the patient has been speaking very fast. When asking the patient if anything seems different, the patient denies anything wrong, only adding that, “she’s made great progress on her plans." The patient said she has felt like this on one occasion 2 years ago, and she recalled being hospitalized for about 2 weeks. She denies any history of depression, although she said about a year ago she had no energy and had a hard time motivating herself to go to class and see her friends for months. She denies hearing any voices or any visual hallucinations. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "History of manic episode 2 years ago" -> "Current manic symptoms (elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity)" -> "Denies history of depression" -> "Denies auditory or visual hallucinations" -> "Likely diagnosis: Bipolar I disorder" -> 80%

CHAIN: "History of low energy and lack of motivation about a year ago" -> "Current manic symptoms (elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity)" -> "Denies history of depression" -> "Denies auditory or visual hallucinations" -> "Likely diagnosis: Bipolar I disorder" -> 75%
enhanced_information: The patient's history of a manic episode 2 years ago, current manic symptoms, denial of depression, and absence of hallucinations suggest a likely diagnosis of Bipolar I disorder. The evidence paths do not provide additional relevant information for this case.
analysis: The patient's presentation with a history of a previous manic episode, current manic symptoms, denial of depression, absence of hallucinations, and the enhanced information pointing towards Bipolar I disorder strongly suggest this diagnosis. Bipolar I disorder is characterized by manic episodes, which the patient is currently experiencing, along with a history of a previous manic episode. The absence of depressive symptoms and hallucinations further support this diagnosis over other mood disorders.
